It is surely hardly arguable that the rule can be applied in such a way that you would have a regular interruption of the ordinary business of the house on this alleged matter of urgency each time the statistics came out, especially when you realize that there will be other occasions, and early occasions, when the matter can be discussed.

One does not for a moment say that the situation is not serious. In dealing with this application to interrupt our ordinary proceedings of this day under standing order 26 in order to embark on a discussion of "the grave unemployment situation in the country as revealed in a government press announcement made today," I remind hon. members that this is not a new problem for the Chair. Unfortunately the problem of unemployment is a continuing one and has been a continuing one. As I recall it, motions of this kind have been advanced or attempts have been made to deal with the general problem of unemployment under standing order 26, and I have taken the view in the past that that

is not an appropriate procedure for a continuing general problem which this undoubtedly is.
I have had a good deal of assistance from members on both sides of the house. The argument is that the figures released today have created an urgency of debate which did not exist, for example, when the house met on January 14 or in the intervening time when, as I recall the course of debate not only on the address in reply to the speech from the throne but at other opportunities, a great deal was said about unemployment in general. In fact if the pages of Hansard which deal with this general problem of unemployment were added together I think they would be found to have occupied a fair part of the time of the house to this point.
I do not want to work any hardship on any hon. member who disagrees with me, but in line with the view I have taken in the past I cannot do other than reject this as an appropriate motion to be interposed at this stage under standing order 26.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Department of Justice Act to provide for the appointment of two associate deputy ministers of justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF TWO ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that the committee will agree with me that there is no need for a lengthy explanation of this resolution. I should perhaps make a brief statement as to some of the considerations moving the government to introduce the resolution and then would be glad to answer any questions that may be directed to me.
The main consideration which warrants the proposal contained in the resolution is, of course, the increase in the volume of work done by the Department of Justice and the increased importance of the status of that work. With regard to the second part of the proposition, I immediately disclaim any personal responsibility. I am not saying that it depends on the minister. It is a fact, however, that by virtue of the increasing complexity and scope of the government business bringing the government, as it does, into contact with outside organizations in a way that was perhaps not the case in earlier years there has been a change and steady development in the nature and the responsibility of the work undertaken by the Department of Justice for other departments of the government and for the government as a whole in connection with the legal advice, counsel and representation that must be afforded the government in the discharge of that work and in the official relationships on a legal basis that ensue from the nature of that work.
With regard to the first heading of the proposition which I put forward, I think the facts speak for themselves. I have some statistics if hon. members would be interested in them but I do not think it requires much elaboration to emphasize the fact that the size of government is growing with the increase in population, that the volume of government work naturally has grown as a result of and along with the increase in population, the broadening of the nature of the work done by the government and as a result of the increase

Department of Justice Act in the number and the nature of the relationships between governments and the citizens and organizations of the country.
It is as a reflection of these symptoms that the government has felt it appropriate to recommend that there be provision made in the department for the appointment of two associate deputy ministers of justice, into which positions it is intended to move initially the two officers who now occupy the positions of assistant deputy ministers.
I know that these two gentlemen would not wish me to dwell at length upon their qualifications because they are modest civil servants in every sense of the word but I cannot let this opportunity go by without expressing to the committee and through the committee to the country my very real sense of appreciation and that of the government as a whole for the quality of the work and advice given by these two senior officers of my department. I know that those on the other side of the house who have had experience in government will fully agree with what I say when I speak in the highest possible terms of the work of these two officers and the contribution which their work has assisted the Department of Justice to the business of government as a whole over the past number of years.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF TWO ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some members of the committee may recall that in the late spring of 1957 the prime minister of that day, Mr. St. Laurent, announced his intention of asking parliament to approve of the appointment of two associate deputy ministers of justice and if subsequent circumstances had permitted that step would have been taken by him. Therefore the committee will not be surprised if I indicate that we wholeheartedly support the resolution which has just been introduced by the Minister of Justice. Our support for the resolution is all the more wholehearted because of the minister's announcement of the intention of the government, if the resolution and the subsequent bill are carried, to appoint to these new positions the assistant deputy ministers of the department. I agree with him that they have served the government and the country faithfully and well and that they are eminently suited for these posts. If they are appointed to them they will carry, I know, the good will of all members of the house in the new responsibilities which they have earned.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I might add one word. In view of the fact that traditionally the appointment of deputy ministers and associate deputy ministers has been the prerogative of the prime minister, perhaps it

might have been appropriate for a resolution and bill of this kind to come to the house in the name of the Prime Minister, but I am not making any particular point of that question of procedure. In any event we warmly support the resolution and commend the minister on the step he has recommended and particularly on the appointments he proposes to make if the resolution and the bill are carried.

speechtext: I think this is really a question of semantics in calling them associate deputy ministers. At the present time they are assistant deputy ministers and the title will be changed to associate deputy ministers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF TWO ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS
speechtext: That last sentence is correct, yes. I should like to make one point clear before the resolution carries. I appreciate the comments of the Leader of the Opposition. I was aware, of course, of the announcement made by the former prime minister of his intention and that of his government had they been returned in 1957, and it is obvious of course that I share the views which the former prime minister held. While not in any sense wishing to differ from or criticize what was said on that occasion by the former prime minister, I want to make it perfectly clear that I and the present government have reached this decision on our own. We are recommending this because of our knowledge and experience of the quality of the work done by these two officers and because of our knowledge and experience of the nature of the work required to be done in these positions. Perhaps, therefore, I should really leave it on the basis that members of the former government and the present government have in this matter reached a pleasant harmony of view.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF TWO ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a question. When the discussion was taking place on the necessity of this decision, did he And, or was there found, any general over-all principle in relation to this kind of appointment in so far as it would apply to other departments, or was there any tradition in the past, or was it just a decision based almost

wholly upon the problems of the Department of Justice? I might explain that the reason I ask this question has to do with the situation in the Department of Transport, which I think could probably stand several more associate deputy ministers; that is, in terms of the size of the organization. I am wondering whether there is any principle or any past practice that has relation to the Department of Justice and on which the minister could comment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF TWO ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, at least our decision was not based on that. There have been instances in the past where there have been associate deputy ministers of other departments. I think particularly of the Department of National Defence, where there was provision for the position of associate deputy minister; I think that when the Department of Defence Production was first set up there was also provision for an associate deputy minister; but, I must say, that in the present case the decision has been made on the basis of the nature and quality of the work done and required to be done in the Department of Justice.
The fact of the matter is that, with the possible exception of the Department of Finance, the Department of Justice enters more directly into and has more direct relationships with the work of all the other departments of government than does any other single department. It is the responsibility of this department to advise all other departments, and to draft the legislation of all other departments. All other departments come to us with respect to their legal problems, and these are multitudinous, so that the relationship between the Department of Justice and every other department of government is constant and important and, I am happy to say, very pleasant and cordial.
I think that is one of the prime reasons why it is more appropriate to have associate deputy ministers in the Department of Justice than it would perhaps be in the case of other departments, because of the volume and nature of our relationships with every other department of government and the fact that these relationships are frequently carried on at a relatively high level, the level of relatively senior officers of departments. For these reasons it seems appropriate to confirm -I will not say to improve, because it would be difficult to have more pleasant relationship-an appropriate change to make to introduce positions for two associate deputy ministers in the Department of Justice.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OP INSURED LOANS, ETC.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OP INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1954 to increase the aggregate amount of all loans in respect of which insurance policies may be issued under the Act from four billion dollars to six billion dollars; and to increase from one billion dollars to one and a half billion dollars the aggregate amount that may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund for the purposes specified in subsection 1 of section 22 of the said act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Flynn in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OP INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a resolution preceding the introduction of a bill to amend the National Housing Act. May I first say how pleased I am, after having been interested in low cost housing for 25 years, and having seen the lower part of my riding of Rosedale redeemed so that it is now one of the show places on the continent of low rental housing, to have the opportunity of acting as a minister of the crown reporting to the house on national housing.
May I very briefly review the history of the housing field in the past two and one-half years? When this government came to power in 1957 our economy was headed toward a recession. The general economic situation, and the housing situation in particular, clearly pointed to the need for vigorous action on the part of the government. The housing industry was suffering almost worse than any other industry and had declined ever since the third quarter of 1955. By the first quarter of 1957, the annual rate of housing had reached a 5-year low of
86,000	units.

National Housing Act
Prospective home owners were finding it almost impossible to finance a home. The ordinary citizen, who was in the low third of our income groups, could not finance a home. The rapidly worsening employment situation was aggravated by the falling off of home construction. In spite of this, nothing was done of a serious nature at that time to stimulate the construction industry, long recognized as the bulwark and one of the most important methods of increasing employment.
Under section 22 of the National Housing Act, 1954 the previous government authorized the lending of $250 million. When the Diefen-baker government took office three years later, only $100 million of this amount had been granted for mortgage lending. The policy of the previous government restricted the regulations under which central mortgage could lend to certain selected areas, as the authorities on the other side of the house are so well aware. As a result of this, the need for small homes for families in the lower income group in our great metropolitan areas was sadly neglected. When this government took office we immediately released the additional $150 million then available under the National Housing Act to foster the building of small homes.
Under the new small home loans program we gave careful consideration to the problems of the lower income group. We felt then, and I would say rightly, that loans should only be approved for units that did not exceed a certain size limit. We amended the 1954 act so that National Housing Act loans could be granted for 90 per cent of the first $12,000 and 70 per cent of the balance up to $12,800. This had the effect, generally, of increasing loans and thereby reducing the down payment necessary on a house. The government was more concerned with the requirements, as I say, of borrowers in the low income group who had modest housing intentions than with the requirements of the more fortunate and wealthier people who could afford to do their financing through conventional channels.
The housing situation at the end of 1957, as a result of the new policy of the government and the manner in which it was put into force, stood in dramatic contrast to what we found on coming into power in June. The rate of house-building, for instance, had increased from a first quarter annual rate of
86,000	units to a record rate of 150,000 units in the final quarter so that there were 122,000 starts in 1957. Employment opportunities in the winter of 1957-58 had been greatly brightened by the 14,000 additional housing starts under the small homes loan program in the fall of the year. New opportunities,

for the first time, presented themselves for people of modest means to obtain their own homes. This had a tremendous effect on the morale of tens of thousands of people who wanted to have their own homes. The earlier lacklustre pace of the industry had changed to one of unprecedented activity, and the uncertain midsummer outlook had changed to one of vigorous confidence.
The great success of this, to which I give due credit to the distinguished Secretary of State for External Affairs who formerly was the minister reporting to the house on this program, was proven beyond a doubt when before the end of 1957 the remaining $150 million available under the 1954 act had been taken up by builders and home owners. In December of 1957 the government, therefore, increased, with the consent of this house, the total amount of money available under the act from $250 million to $400 million, and in May of 1958 the amount available under the act was raised again to $750 million. I do not need to tell hon. members of the house, because on the opposite side I can see two or three authorities who know this full well, of the great improvement in home construction which resulted from this fillip to the building industry, which helped to provide jobs for hundreds of thousands of Canadians. I think all those on the other side of the house will realize in retrospect that this courageous program was one of the most important factors in the recovery of our economy from the 1958 recession.
May I now report very briefly on 1959, the year which has just passed. As a whole, it was a good year for housing, a very good year, with housing starts numbering 141,000. This is a figure that no one ever heard of before 1957, and is the second highest on record. The completions for the same year amounted to 145,000, higher than ever before. In order to finance this program, and that is what we are here to do, the government again amended section 22 of the National Housing Act on March 20, 1959 and again increased the amount available under the act to $1 billion. Although 1959 was considered a most successful year in housing I feel that I must point out that during the latter part of the year there was a progressive and steady withdrawal of private lenders from insured lending under the act. This resulted in a very serious problem which faced me when I took over this portfolio at the end of August, 1959. As this country recovered from the recession a rise in personal expenditure and the demand for long term funds to finance our increased economic activity caused a considerable drain on the funds available for mortgage lending. This

resulted in a rise in long term interest rates and a diminished attractiveness of the 6 per cent National Housing Act rate.
At the end of 1959-it was an amazing thing to watch-the approved lenders had clearly retired from the insured lending field. For instance, in the year 1959 the number of units on which approved lenders had made loans had dropped from 46,000 in 1958 to
25,000.	In order to offset this decline in insured lending Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation stepped up its direct lending. Hon. members of the house will appreciate that this heavy direct lending program during the latter months of 1959 was justified in order to prevent a precipitous decline and in order to maintain employment or at least make the contribution which the housing industry could make to employment during this winter. This demand for central mortgage and housing direct loans in the fall of 1959 was so great that by the end of October the corporation had sufficient applications on hand to commit essentially the funds available under section 22 of the National Housing Act and they decided they must stop accepting new applications.
I should like to point out at this time it was not because the government ran out of money. It was very much a case of applications for loans being so great that the government felt it was best to parcel out the remaining money to the existing applicants. It was almost like the east-west game, the Grey cup final, where the box office is open for a week but when it is sold out in two days they close the office but the tickets are still there and the game is still to be played. That is the way it was with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. As a matter of fact, those loans are still being processed.
I now come to the final development of the policy for 1959 and that is the increase in the maximum interest rate allowable on insured loans under the National Housing Act. I expect and I welcome discussion on this matter from all sides of the house. This rate was raised in December of last year from 6 per cent to 6| per cent in order once more to prompt a greater flow of private money into national housing mortgages during this year 1960.
I do not mind saying-and hon. members will know this-that the government came very reluctantly to the decision to raise the interest rate in order to procure more private money because we have always regarded the protection of the borrower as one of the main purposes of the National Housing Act and we are disappointed at any development that forces additional financial burdens 79951-0-74J
National Housing Act
upon the borrower. But we had the choice in this instance-and you can see it-between virtually no loans whatever under the act from the private lenders at 6 per cent or an appreciable flow-at least we hope it will be an appreciable flow-at 6J per cent. I might say that we had a great deal of difficulty in arriving at the rate of 6J per cent. It had to be attractive enough to get back into the market of the approved lenders and yet we had to hold it down as much as possible in order to protect the borrowers or the would-be home owners.
No doubt many people would have preferred the government to support this housing program by maintaining at the accelerated rate its direct Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation lending at the very high level of the previous two years, if that were possible. But as you can see, for reasons which far transcend the reasons in my own department-for reasons of government-it is not possible to keep on indefinitely lending money in such large amounts. The provision of public money on a large scale for mortgage lending has important fiscal implications which most hon. members of the house realize, adding as it does to the cash requirements of the government and contributing to cash deficits.
At times government cash deficits are appropriate to prevailing economic conditions and we feel that the economic circumstances of 1957, 1958 and, to a lesser extent, 1959 justify the policy of public lending to support house building. We look forward in 1960, however, to a year of comparatively full use of our national economic resources and a year in which the benefits of mortgage lending by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation must be weighed against the broader fiscal difficulties which would be raised by continuing to make the funds available through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation on the same scale as in the years 1958 and 1959.
We feel too that the present economic outlook for 1960 calls for a substantial decline in C.M.H.C. lending in the hope that by raising the interest rate to 6j per cent we can get a greater percentage participation from the approved lenders.
In the light of this outlook, and in view of the withdrawal of private lenders from insured lending at 6 per cent, we considered it necessary to prompt a higher rate of lending by permitting the private lenders a higher yield on National Housing Act mortgages. Even with this higher interest rate, Mr. Chairman, lending by the private lenders under the act may not be even as high as in 1959 when loans for 25,000 units were approved. There will no doubt be an increase in the

National Housing Act
participation of life insurance companies, mortgage companies and trust companies who approved insured loans for about 11,000 units in 1959. But the position of the banks, who approved loans for 14,000 units in 1959 and who did very little lending in the last few months of the year, is uncertain. It is unlikely that private insured loans in 1960 in any event will be much higher than in 1959 and C.M.H.C. direct loans are likely to be a good deal lower.
While there will be some decline in housing starts in 1960, completions will still be substantial. It will cheer the house to know that there are at the present time, largely owing to the winter program and to other factors, about 80,000 uncompleted units still under construction at the beginning of this year 1960, new housing which will be continuing to come on to the market at a high rate for some time to come. That is good news because they will be absorbed and will act as a cushion to cutting down the amount of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation direct loans.
Although heavy governmental expenditures and government deficits are appropriate in times of recession, I think we will all agree that under normal circumstances government expenditures should be limited to our income. In view of this consideration we felt it necessary to raise the insured lending rate from 6 per cent to 6f per cent in order to attract, as I said before, mortgage funds from private lending and thus relieve the burden on the taxpayer.
There are one or two points that I should like to make on the resolution and then I am looking forward to a great deal of help and assistance and questions from both sides of the house, either in this resolution stage or at the second reading stage, whatever hon. members prefer. But the resolution before us which all hon. members have-and it is to be found at page 10 of the orders of the day-has as its main purpose the increasing of the appropriation under section 22 of the National Housing Act. This appropriation sets the limit on the amount the government may lend to C.M.H.C. to carry out its mortgage lending policy. I have already explained how this appropriation, originally set at $250 million, has now been increased to $1 billion and how that $1 billion was finally all committed by October, 1959. It is now proposed to increase this appropriation by $500 million, from $1,000 to $1,500 million, in order to permit the continuation of mortgage lending by C.M.H.C. for some time to come.
I want to emphasize that this additional sum of $500 million is intended to last for some time. I have already explained to hon. members that present circumstances argue for a

considerable reduction in C.M.H.C. lending in 1960. Last year the corporation committed about $350 million for mortgage lending purposes. That is a very large sum. I wanted to take this opportunity to draw your attention to the difficult problem facing the corporation and to avoid raising the expectation in any quarter that the $500 million increase proposed in the appropriation indicates a readiness on the part of this government to continue mortgage lending through C.M.H.C. on the scale experienced in the last two years, and I believe you can appreciate that.
The second part of the resolution deals with section 13 of the act and the limit of $4 billion now imposed on the amount of mortgages the C.M.H.C. may insure. As lenders are likely to ask the corporation to go beyond this $4 billion mark in the early part of 1960, or at some time in 1960, we are asking parliament for authority-as you see, this resolution is in two parts-to increase the figure to $6 billion. This is not an authority for expenditures, as hon. members of the house will realize; it relates to the amount of mortgage debt that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation may insure, not the amount of mortgage loans it may make.
Having concluded by chronology the past two and a half years, and having spoken briefly on the proposed amendments, I should like to beg your indulgence, if I may, for a little bit longer to comment upon the government's policy from a more topical point of view. Over the past three years the total number of starts in Canada has averaged
143,000	a year, this average being higher than the starts in any single preceding year. We have it as a main objective to maintain over the years an average rate of new building-I ask hon. members of this house to consider this important-in excess of that rate necessary to keep up with the increase and movement of population in the country. Currently it requires something of the order of 125,000 new dwellings in Canada each year to meet the needs arising out of family formations, the increase in other kinds of households, the destruction and loss of dwellings, and the persistent drift of population from rural to urban areas. There is only one way to obtain improvements in the national stock of housing, and that is to build houses somewhat faster than the need for them grows and then to maintain and keep them in good shape. There may be years in which it is difficult to maintain a rate of building that would be considered adequate over the long run if continued. The important thing, however, is to compensate for such periods in other years, and to maintain a satisfactory average rate of building over the years.

Over much of the past decade the demand for mortgage money at N.H.A. borrowing rates has been far in excess of the available supply, but this government has demonstrated its willingness, when other conditions allow, to devote public funds on a very large scale to N.H.A. mortgage lending in all parts of the country. Since the government came to power in 1957 Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has made mortgage loans under the act in an amount close to $900 million.
I may say at this stage how pleased I was on reading over the debates of previous years at the contributions made by hon. members in this house. This housing problem we have tried to keep as much as possible non-political, and we have had a great deal of assistance from both sides of the house in this regard. But there are times, of course, when broader fiscal considerations require a moderation of government mortgage lending, and at such times it may prove necessary, as it has recently, to evoke a greater flow of private and institutional mortgage funds, as I said before.
In the provision of mortgage money out of public funds, however, we have always used methods intended to direct the assistance to the lower income ranges of eligible N.H.A. borrowers. The lower income groups will continue to arouse the greatest concern of this corporation and, of course, of the government, even if these lower income borrowers can only afford housing of a kind that some wealthier critics of the government have said nobody wants. Our concern with the lower income groups has been manifest in the requirement that only modest accommodation will be built with C.M.H.C. loans, in the lowering of down payment requirements and in the authorization of higher ratios of mortgage debt to income at the same time.
In conclusion, may I say just one word on the subject of housing for lower income families. I know that I will be asked questions about this, and I will be delighted to answer them within the scope of my limited ability. It is appropriate for me to draw the attention of hon. members to the activities in urban redevelopment and in public housing that this government has supported under the National Housing Act during the past two and a half years. In the field of urban redevelopment a great deal of interest is being shown and activity has quickened considerably.
Urban redevelopment projects are often preceded by studies which identify those areas of a city which are ripe for clearance and redevelopment. The government aids such studies financially under part V of the National Housing Act, and in the past two and
National Housing Act
a half years 19 cities across Canada have been given financial assistance of this kind. That is a large number of cities. Prior to this period -I am not making any comparison except to point out how this matter has been stepped up

only some half a dozen studies were undertaken.
As a result of these studies, actual redevelopment projects are under way in a number of centres, notably Halifax, Windsor and Toronto. Earlier projects in Toronto, Montreal and St. John's have been completed or are nearing completion. In all these cities the federal government has undertaken to give financial assistance under section 23 of the act up to the extent of 50 per cent of the total cost of the undertaking.
At the present time preliminary investigations are under way in connection with housing projects involving some 2,200 low rental units. In addition projects involving more than 3,600 rental housing units have already been given final approval or are presently under construction. This program is the largest so far undertaken under the well known section 36 of the National Housing Act.
In summarizing the housing measures of this government over the past two and a half years, I would suggest, has had three main features, each of which is new. First, there has been recognition of the basic fact that the total program must be maintained over the long pull at a rate high enough to bring about improvements in the over-all housing situation. Second, in pursuing this aim the government has shown no categorical reluctance to use Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation as a major lender when this does not interfere with the adoption of a sound fiscal policy. Finally, in the disposition of government mortgage funds we have always been careful to adopt policies which tend to divert these funds to the use of the lower income families within the range of eligible borrowers.

I ask this question because I have not been able to find any striking indication that the income level of those taking advantage of N.H.A. mortgages has been dropping.

National Housing Act

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OP INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am very much obliged to the hon. member tor asking this question. I know the hon. member tor Port Arthur is particularly interested in the lower income groups, and he will be pleased to know that with regard to the income of N.H.A. borrowers in 1959, of the total number of loans made 52.6 per cent were to people with incomes of less than $5,000. In a moment I will get for him how that compares with the previous year. To continue: those earning less than $6,000 but more than $5,000, 24.9 per cent; those with incomes less than $7,000 and above $6,000, 12.1 per cent; and those earning $7,000 and over, 10.4 per cent. Thus, hon. members can see that this is a small home loans program. Out of 100 per cent of the loans granted, 52.6 per cent were for people with incomes lower than $5,000.
On the other hand, the figures show that the other corporation loans-the loans made throughout the country other than those in the metropolitan areas-were divided as follows: the percentage of those obtaining loans whose incomes are under $5,000 is 51.9 per cent, which is almost the same as the figure I gave a moment ago. The other figures are approximately the same, whereas in the case of the approved lenders, we find' that the percentage of loans going to those with incomes of less than $5,000 is 28.6. Does that answer the hon. member's question?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OP INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to take this
opportunity to convey to the new Minister of Public Works our heartiest congratulations and best wishes on the occasion of the new responsibility which has fallen to him. I was able to offer my personal congratulations at the time of his appointment, but this is the first opportunity I have had to say publicly how pleased I am to know that one who is reportedly as close to the Prime Minister as the hon. gentleman is should be in charge of this important portfolio.
Without detracting in any way from the reputation of the many excellent ministers

of public works we have had in the past, perhaps at this time I may refer particularly to the minister's two predecessors who also had the responsibility of reporting to this house on behalf of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. 1 am, of course, referring to the present Secretary of State for External Affairs and to the Hon. Robert Winters who were a credit to the department. We wish the new minister an enjoyable tenure of office and-I know he will appreciate the spirit in which we say this-we hope it will not be too prolonged.
The resolution before us divides itself into two distinct parts. First, to increase the aggregate amount of all loans in respect to which insurance policies may be issued under the act from $4 billion to $6 billion and, second, to increase from $1 billion to $1,500 million the aggregate amount that may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund for the purposes specified in subsection 1 of section 22 of the said act.
One's immediate reaction to this proposed legislation is that the government obviously intends to increase the limit as to insured loans and to increase the lending authority of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to a point in each case where it will not be necessary for the government even to discuss housing policy at the next session of parliament, or indeed for what well may be the duration of this parliament. If one may judge by what has been said in the press- and that seems to be the place to learn of this government's policy-C.M.H.C. loans in 1960 are not likely to exceed $175 million.
Therefore, what we are being asked to approve in this parliament is really a two or two and a half year supply of mortgage loans if this proposed rate of assistance is to be provided. What we are being asked to do is to give this government a blank cheque in this field that they may use at their own discretion between now and the next election. Further, in asking for this blank cheque they seem determined to avoid any debate on this subject between now and the next election. I think this was confirmed by what the minister had to say today. This course of action on the part of the government seems to be a far cry from their utterances when they were in the opposition.
In so far as insured loans are concerned, total N.H.A. loans have never exceeded $908 million-the 1958 total-so that a $2 billion increase as proposed in this legislation will quite obviously leave the government plenty of leeway and make it unnecessary for it to ask for fresh parliamentary authority.

There is certainly nothing in today's housing situation to justify any degree of complacency. I think this government has been far too eager to over-publicize the seasonally adjusted rate of house construction in September and October. The truth of the matter is that housing starts in 1959 are down from 1958, and from the most expert opinion as expressed by the industry across the country housing will be down substantially more in 1960. The degree to which it will be restricted will depend on the actions of this government because, whether they like it or not, they are now in the housing business up to their ears.
I would like to remind the house briefly of the spotty, unplanned, on-and-off course this government has followed in the field of mortgage funds for housing, having in mind that the provision of an adequate and steady flow of mortgage funds to the housebuilding industry is one of the major problems facing that important industry. Practically ever since the time this government took office the housebuilding industry has been in a state of feast or famine in respect to the availability of mortgage funds. This situation has been brought about by lack of planning and, in particular, by the fiscal and monetary policies followed by this government. Let me point out just a few instances.
In the winter of 1957-58, with the worst unemployment situation this country has faced since the depression of the thirties, this government ran out of funds during the election campaign. Promises were made, of course, and money was approved, but not until the following May. In the meantime much of the industry and the people who could have been employed stood idle. Then more millions were poured into it.
Let us, for a moment, look at the situation last summer. Despite several attempts on this side of the house to have the government make its intentions known in respect to direct loans, the matter was held in abeyance by the government until parliament prorogued on July 18. Then, on July 22, the Prime Minister announced resumption of this small loan program which, I point out, had been lying dormant since the previous January. The Prime Minister's statement contained the following and I quote:
This year's quota of 15 loans to qualified builders will be made available from September 1 to December 31
The Prime Minister continued:
Small home loans will be available to builders who were in business on June 1, 1959, and who are unable to obtain the assistance they require under the usual insured mortgage loan arrangements.
National Housing Act
The Prime Minister's announcement went on to say, and I quote:
Re-introduction of the program of direct loans to builders-
I would like to underline the next lines of this quotation:
-will in no way affect the present policy of residual loans by C.M.H.C. to prospective home owners.
Following the Prime Minister's announcement, Canadian housing statistics, published by C.M.H.C., and which reached us on October 29, said with regard to direct loans to builders and I quote:
Such loans are to be available, however, from September 1 to the end of the year. By the end of August, applications have been received for these loans for close to 6,000 dwelling units.
Despite these positive statements-that of the Prime Minister and that of C.M.H.C.- the Minister of Public Works announced on October 30 that new applications from builders, home owners, or limited dividend companies could not be accepted after the close of business that day. The minister's announcement, of which no notice was given, was a complete repudiation of the terms and conditions outlined by the Prime Minister. In view of these firm commitments, it was clear that the sudden shutting off of this important supply of mortgage money took builders generally by surprise and was another indication of the confused and fumbling methods which the government seems to follow.
This sudden closing of the door against new loan applications was detrimental to the individual home owner in smaller centres who, unable to secure mortgage loans under the National Housing Act from a bank or the normal lending institutions, was no longer able to turn to the government agency for a direct loan. These people were then faced with paying higher interest rates for conventional loans or cancelling their plans to build homes altogether.
At that time I pointed out that this untimely mess, and it was untimely just as we headed into a period when we might expect some increase in unemployment, was the direct responsibility of this government. The government, by mismanagement of its own finances, had created a tight money and a high interest situation. This shutting off of mortgage funds was the direct result of the monetary and fiscal policies followed by the government.
It is common knowledge that the large cash deficits of the government started a chain reaction. To obtain the cash it needed the government mopped up funds available for investing, thereby pushing up rates of interest to unprecedented high levels and bringing down the value not only of its own

National Homing Act
securities but of all securities. The setting up of high interest rates for government bonds made it necessary to establish higher rates of interest on other investments so as to make the return they provided competitive with returns from government securities.
Mortgage investments, which are admittedly more costly to administer, have always commanded about 1 per cent higher rate than government securities. This fully explains the high interest rates now being charged on conventional loans. Conventional loans on mortgages are now being made at per cent and 8 per cent and in some cases 8J per cent-I had an example of that in the past week-with discounts on second mortgages running as high as 50 per cent. Imagine the position that puts a wage earner in when he not necessarily loses his job but is faced with the problem of reduced income. The government in these cases has helped to create in many areas of Canada virtual loan sharks' paradise.
Naturally, with interest rates soaring, money was siphoned off from housing, much of it by this government's own borrowings. Then with interest rates climbing an increasing number of house builders had to turn to direct loans. It is little wonder that the tremendous sum of $1 billion voted by parliament was exhausted prematurely. This is simply another example of lack of planning and lack of good judgment by this government stumbling along from crisis to crisis, many of them of their own making.
This turning on and turning off the tap in respect of mortgage funds for house building is further proof of the lack of any sound government policy in respect of housing despite the hundreds of millions that have been provided by parliament and, at the same time, creates confusion in the industry. Erratic outbursts of house building with mortgage funds available at the whim or fancy of a government can only add to the already high cost of housing. I repeat, the house building industry is dependent upon, and I emphasize this, a steady flow of mortgage funds.
Let me refer briefly to the government's policy on interest rates for National Housing Act loans. On May 26, 1959, as recorded at page 4012 of Hansard, the Minister of Public Works assured the commons that the existing interest rate of 6 per cent for National Housing Act mortgage loans would not be increased. He gave that assurance to the house in response to a question by me on that date. May I now move along to October 5, 1959, and a Canadian Press story appearing in the Globe and Mail on October 6, which goes on to say that it appears unlikely there will be any 
increase in the government's mortgage lending rate despite current high interest rates in other fields and a decline in new housing starts to date. The story quotes the Minister of Public Works as saying this:
I certainly know of no government plans to raise the National Housing Act interest rates.
These were his exact words. The next development was the minister's announcement of December 17 that effective immediately the interest rate on National Housing Act loans would be boosted from 6 per cent to 6g per cent. This action, taken by order in council, established the highest rate of interest ever charged since the institution of the National Housing Act.
At that time I pointed out that this latest hike in rates would mean approximately an extra $7.50 per month interest on each $12,800 N.H.A. approved loan. It could also mean another $6 to $8 per month rent for the average sized new apartment. As is usually the case, these extra costs will have to be borne by the people that can least afford it, the lower income groups.
At that time, one week before Christmas, I pointed out that this was a most unwelcome Christmas present and cited it as another example of the results of what has now become so well and so properly known as "Fleming's Folly", the government's financially imprudent but obviously politically necessary conversion loan of 1958.
While we are on the subject of increasing interest rates and their effect on housing, I should like to put on the record the views of no less an authority than the present Minister of Finance to the effect that increasing interest rates can only deter construction. I would refer you to Hansard of April 23, 1956, page 3171, where the minister was referring to an increase in the National Housing Act rate of one quarter of one per cent. The present Minister of Finance had this to say at that time:
I am led by this increase in the rate, by government decision to ask: Is the government seeking to reduce the rate of house construction in Canada?
A little further on, at the bottom of the same page, he made this statement, and I am again quoting:
I am bound to point out that an increase in the interest rate normally has the effect and usually is intended to have the effect of restraining house construction.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member the year of that quotation?

speechtext:
It is page 3171 of Hansard, 1956. I wonder how the minister would reconcile his position at that time with his government's decision to boost the interest rate on N.H.A. loans, not by the one quarter

of 1 per cent to which he was referring at that time but by three times this rate of increase to 6J per cent as announced by the government a few weeks ago.
I could go on. The Minister of Finance grew stronger in his objection to raising the interest rate because three days later on April 26, 1956, as reported at page 3307 of Hansard, at the second reading stage, the minister had this to say:
The effect of an increase in interest rate necessarily is to make construction more expensive, to increase carrying charges, and to that extent to reduce the volume of home construction that would otherwise be attained.
As I mentioned, the minister made these outbursts against a quarter of one per cent raise in the interest rate on N.H.A. loans. Yet on December 18 he supported an increase of three times as much at a time when other departments were reportedly trying to increase rather than decrease employment opportunities.

speechtext: I know that the hon. member for Nipissing wants to be fair. Does he not recall that his government in a period of less than 12 months raised the interest rate three quarters of one per cent?

speechtext: I am simply pointing out what the present Minister of Finance said about an increase of one quarter of one per cent and I am relating that to his position taken a few weeks ago with regard to an increase of three times the magnitude.

speechtext: Consistency is not the main characteristic of the Minister of Finance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OP INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Surely there can be no better example, if we can rely on the minister's sincerity, and I am not questioning that, of the inconsistency in the policies of this government; on the one hand claiming to be trying to create winter employment and at the same time, according to the theory of the Minister of Finance, trying to restrict house construction.
It would seem to us, in view of the many uncertainties created in the past two and a half years as to government plans and in view of the substantial portion of mortgage funds supplied by this government, that surely the government owes it to the industry, to the financial community and to the public generally, to reveal now in this debate precisely what their plans are for 1960.
We are prepared to support the government's request for this substantial increase in the hope that making these funds available will remove many of the uncertainties occasioned by the turning on and shutting off the supply of mortgage funds by this government. I would hope the minister will take
National Housing Act
advantage of this debate to spell out in clear, concise terms when the government intends to resume direct lending and the degree of assistance. Such a statement of policy is essential at this time to avoid a further decline in housing starts.
There is another inconsistency which I should like to point out in government policy with respect to housing loans. The government by its action has put the banks out of the mortgage lending field. When one remembers that the banks in this country have supplied a substantial portion of mortgage money since 1954, then one wonders whether this is a further deliberate attempt by the government to curtail house construction. Here again there is need for a clear statement of the government's intention.
It has been clearly indicated, that the decline in residential construction in 1959 has been due to such factors as restricted direct lending by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the tight money condition and high interest rates on government bonds. Therefore, the government is directly responsible for the decline in construction activity in 1959.
A further decline is indicated for 1960 by most industry spokesmen. Government spokesmen seem to toss around the figure of
125,000	starts as an objective. I have been following some of their speeches in the press, and this is the figure they use. The minister used it again today. Unless the government acts promptly and wisely, starts may well be substantially less. We on this side of the house say, surely there is no justification for the house building industry to be singled out for further curtailment in 1960, as a result of the shortcomings of government fiscal policy. We do not believe there is any justification for a government policy of restriction of house construction at this time. It is a well-known fact that house construction provides jobs. With well over 786,000-we received those figures today-of our population seeking employment, there is no justification for the government pursuing policies which can only lessen job opportunities in this country.
Canadian housing statistics, third quarter, at page 18-and I am anxious to add this to the figure supplied by the minister-in a table recording the incomes of applicants under the National Housing Act, show that in the third quarter of 1959 only 8.4 per cent of the total loans were made to people earning under $4,000 a year, or approximately $80 a week. This is a serious state of affairs when we realize that the majority of Canadians in the lower half of the income scale are not benefiting, except in a very limited degree.

National Housing Act
from the provisions of the National Housing Act, the very people this act was intended to assist in securing adequate housing. I realize the government can use statistics and single out certain areas of activity which may make, on the surface, good reading. However, the hard fact remains that the National Housing Act no longer provides the degree of assistance it should to Canadians in the medium and lower income fields.
It is very difficult for us in the opposition to discuss at this stage what the government really intends to do in the field of housing this year until we have seen the bill. We know, of course, that the government intends to provide more money for those who wish and can afford to buy a new house but who do not have the funds required and could not easily secure those funds through the ordinary market mechanism. There is certainly a need for loans guaranteed or made directly by the government in order to meet the situation of this category of people. Such government action, however, provides assistance only for new developments and to those citizens who can afford to own a house. It is therefore very limited indeed, because it does little to meet the serious problem of slums and to help those people who most need government assistance and who cannot afford to own a house.
The existence of slums and of inadequate incomes, together with the difficulties experienced by displaced people as a result of new housing projects constitute the most serious social aspects of the housing problem in our country at the present time. Apparently the bill to be introduced by the government does not contemplate any new action to deal with this most pressing social problem.
Of course, the existing legislation introduced by the former Liberal government contains several specific sections designed to deal with this situation. In particular, section 23 of the act provides contributions up to 50 per cent of the cost to municipalities of acquisition and clearance of blighted or substandard areas. Moreover, section 36 of the act provides for federal contributions of 75 per cent of the capital cost of construction of housing projects for sale or for rent undertaken jointly with provinces or their agencies. However, the construction of main sewers, water mains and streets is not included in the capital cost to be shared by the federal government. Very little has been done under those provisions. Because of the high cost of acquiring and clearing blighted or substandard areas, many municipalities have been unable to take advantage of the enabling provisions of the National Housing Act respecting urban redevelopment and low rental housing.
Even in those municipalities where such projects have been implemented, they have

been on a relatively small scale compared with the need for such projects. While most municipal governments are strongly disposed to undertake redevelopment and re-housing projects, it is felt that the present federal financial aid in such undertakings is inadequate to encourage and facilitate the municipalities in moving forward with redevelopment and low rental housing plans. By assuming a larger share of the costs of acquiring or clearing blighted or substandard areas and low rental housing projects, and by advancing the municipalities' share, to be repayable by the municipalities, a substantial program of such projects throughout Canada could be anticipated.
The Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities recently asked for increased contributions from the federal government in this field. I would like to quote from their submission of February, 1958. This is what they had to say:
Extending the participation of the dominion government in low rental housing and urban redevelopment projects under the National Housing Act by substantially increasing the dominion government's share of the cost of acquiring and clearing blighted or substandard areas; and by advancing the municipalities' share of such costs to be repayable by the municipalities; and by increasing the costs of financing main sewers and water mains in new neighbourhood developments within the framework of the redevelopment provisions of the National Housing Act.
I would like to refer to the plan issued by the leader of the Liberal party at the beginning of the last electoral campaign, which contains specific proposals in this respect. Here is what he said on this matter:
There is an urgent need to speed up the redevelopment of blighted areas in our cities. In order to promote this redevelopment we propose to amend the existing legislation to provide for a greater participation by the federal government. In particular, we propose to increase federal participation in slum clearance schemes from 50 per cent to 75 per cent and to provide for federal sharing in the cost of water, sewer and street services in the area concerned. Also we would propose to ease the present restrictions on redevelopment for commercial and other purposes as well as housing, where that is advisable.
This proposal would have two consequences. First, it would increase the contribution of the federal government provided under section 23 to meet the cost of acquisition and clearance of slum areas from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. Moreover, for construction projects of the type envisaged in section 36, the federal share of 75 per cent would be extended to cover the cost of water, sewer, and street services in the area being redeveloped.
These two concrete proposals, if implemented, would go a long way to meet the most serious social aspect of our housing problem and would put the provinces and

the municipalities in a much better financial position to initiate the projects to meet our human needs in this field. However, the government does not seem to be prepared to move in this direction, and we believe it is most regrettable.

He sat in the house from 1954 to 1957, during which time Canada went through two recessions, and during which time the Liberal machine spent only $100 million by way of loans. In a three-year period we have lent $900 million, nine times as much. Is my hon. friend serious in the observations he is making?

You know, Mr. Chairman, hon. members on the other side of the house think that when they are spending money that the mere spending of the dollars is a substitute for policy.

I should like to take this opportunity to renew a suggestion which I made last year. I believe some effort should be made to encourage the establishment of a secondary market in insured loans that would enable the small investor to participate. It would seem that some method could be found to channel this type of investment into mortgage funds. There are many potential investors with amounts varying from a few hundred dollars to a few thousand dollars who cannot conveniently invest directly in mortgages. Many members of the house will recall that in earlier days small investors would jointly participate in purchasing larger mortgages, but this practice, costly and awkward to administer, has waned in popularity and ceased to be an important feature in the mortgage field.
Proposals have been discussed concerning the forming of a company which would buy N.H.A. guaranteed mortgages from banks, life insurance companies and even from central mortgage itself. It has been proposed that the purchase of these mortgages would be financed by selling bonds to individuals as well as corporate investors. The immediate effect of this proposal would be to clear some existing mortgages from the portfolios of the big lenders and enable them to pour more funds into the mortgage lending stream. It is my opinion that this proposal would be
National Housing Act
most helpful in providing additional mortgage funds by taking advantage of investment potential now in the hands of the small investors who have up to now been unable to participate in this field. I understand that most banks and some life insurance companies endorse this proposal. I would be interested to know what attitude the government takes on this subject, and if anything is being done actively by the government to encourage the implementation of such a proposal.
Housing is indeed an important, complex and interesting subject. It is possible to cover but a few of its aspects in remarks of this kind. We believe there are many areas for improvement in respect to the general subject, and many of these aspects will be dealt with in some detail by my colleagues at this stage and at second reading.
May I close on the same note on which I began, by saying that the Liberal party, with its long record of real achievement in the housing field, stands ready to support this government in this legislation to whatever extent it will have the effect of creating one more job or one more housing unit for our people, especially in the lower income brackets.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like the member for Nipissing, I want to offer our congratulations to the minister upon his appointment and to wish him a most successful career in office as long as he is minister. I intend, at the outset, to express our support, in general terms, of the intent of the resolution. However, I believe that it is time we began to think about what we are doing with the taxpayers' money when we are voting ever increasing amounts to be made available to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. As interest rates continue to rise it is inevitable that a greater and greater percentage of the lower income group of Canadians will not be aided by the provisions of this act. On each and every occasion that we do permit an increase in the interest rate we exclude another group of average or below average income Canadians from obtaining any of the benefits of this act.
In that respect at least the actions of governments over the past number of years have been in direct contradiction to the intent of the act when it was originally introduced into this house. We have no intention of opposing the resolution, and we hope we will not have to oppose the bill when we see it. However, the time may come, if this trend continues whereby more and more of the taxpayers' money is used on behalf of those who really do not need the assistance of the government, when we in this group will have to take another hard look

National Housing Act
at this whole program of using the taxpayers' money to provide housing for a limited number who really do not need the assistance.

speechtext:
May I
ask the hon. member a question. The hon. member refers to the lower income group. Would he say below what level he considers the lower income group to be?

speechtext: I believe the hon. member is aware of the fact that over half of the people in Canada do not even earn enough to make them eligible for the payment of income tax. These are the people who we feel ought to be aided when the taxpayers' money is being used to supply housing in Canada. However, each time you add to the monthly payment you automatically, according to the formula in vogue, exclude more and more of the average and below average wage earners of the nation.

speechtext: On a point of information may I ask the hon. member if he lumps into that group all those single women who are wage earners and therefore would not be considered as being in the category of people about whom we are talking now, that is potential purchasers of homes?

speechtext:
I do not want to get involved in the details. I was attempting to enunciate over-all, general principles. I think even the hon. member for Edmonton West will admit that statistics of even a number of years ago revealed that the vast majority of those who received benefits under this act were people purchasing homes who were in the well paid wage earning bracket or above. I do not believe that particular situation has altered very much. I know the government has made some very commendable moves to make lower priced homes available within recent years. However, rising interest rates have largely offset, if not more than offset, the good intentions of the government in this regard. We have not noted an improvement in the number of people supplied with homes who really need public assistance, as we had hoped.
There is another matter I wish to raise and that is the very future of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The government has now raised the interest rate that is permissible to 6.75 per cent. However, when the government itself has to borrow money and has to pay, as it had to pay last September, as high as 6.8 per cent on the money it needs, it is obvious that there is very little, if any, margin left for what might be a very socially desirable and useful public instrument, the corporation known as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The intention announced, I believe as recently as a year ago, was that the government

would not permit this corporation to operate at a deficit and meet the deficit out of general revenues or out of the consolidated revenue fund. This has caused me considerable concern because I fail to see how the government is able to take this stand when that lending agency is lending money at 6.75 per cent and the government has to pay in the neighbourhood of 6 per cent plus for money.
I hope the government recognizes that this is an institution with which we as a modern society cannot dispense and whose activities and influence ought in no way to be curtailed. If the need arises-and it may not yet have arisen-during the fiscal year for the government to be obliged to face up to the problem, I hope the government will realize the extremely important role this institution may play in our national life and that, if necessary, they will be prepared not only to continue its operation but also to assume enough of the financial burden so that its influence may be extended.

Is he suggesting that we should be charging more on our direct loans and that the approved loans should be at a greater rate of interest than 6f per cent?

speechtext: Oh, no, Mr. Chairman; not at all. For those Canadians who do not need the help of the taxpayers in order to provide themselves with homes we are not overly concerned as to what the rate of interest may be that they might be obliged to pay. We would rather see the government operate Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at a loss in order to enable those who really need public assistance in the matter of housing to receive that assistance. In other words, we would endorse a policy of the government's subsidizing interest rates, if necessary, in order to provide housing for those people for whom we want to obtain housing; and the only instrument or vehicle that we can see essential and necessary to implement such a policy is this instrument we now have, namely Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
