I would submit to the minister that there are far more people in Canada who are in receipt of less than $300 a month or $3,600 per year than there are whose income is in excess of that figure. I submit that those receiving less than $300 per month are the people who are the responsibility of this House of Commons and who are the concern of the public in the matter of housing needs. People receiving in excess of $300 per month and up to $5,000 per annum and more are people whose need in the matter of housing is not nearly as urgent as is that of the man with a family who is receiving less than $300 a month and who under present conditions is completely unable to take advantage of the intent of this act or of the good intentions the minister and the government may have.
We are realizing that events are leading us into a situation in which the exact opposite of declared government policy in the field of financing housing needs is taking place. The government has, over several years now, announced that its policy with regard to finances for housing needs is to encourage an evergrowing participation in this matter on the part of the private money lenders of Canada. Yet despite all the wishes expressed by ministers in the past we realize that a decreasing percentage of the cost of housing is being financed by the private lending institutions of Canada, and for a very good reason, namely that they can make more money by investing their money elsewhere. In some cases they are not obliged to invest their money or tie up their money for as long a term of years as they do in the case of housing.
I think the time has arrived when the government must face up to this trend and must realize that, unless other actions are taken, it is going to continue; it is inevitable, under our expansion economy in which we live at the present time. As long as higher returns with equal security are available in other fields, the investors of Canada cannot really be expected to share the good intentions of the government in the matter of housing and to go along with the wishes of the government merely because they are the expressed wishes of the government.
There have been continuous announcements that government policy is to encourage greater participation by private lending agencies. Yet the facts are that to an evergrowing degree public financing is replacing private lending agencies as the source for the needed housing mortgage money.
The minister may reply with statistics showing that in this month there was more private money for housing than in a corresponding month, but the minister cannot deny
National Housing Act
the fact that, since the Conservative government has taken office in Canada they have deemed it necessary to resort to an evergrowing degree to the use of public finances in order to meet the housing needs of the people of Canada.
I have no particular fault to find with that course. However, it is a contradiction in that the expressed wish of the government is not being met by conditions as they exist and as we continue to find them. The actions of the government really belie their announced policy in that the actions of the government indicate that-in so far as their actions are at least an indication-more and more the whole matter of housing is becoming a social responsibility within the nation and that it must be assumed by the government acting on behalf of the people as a whole.
I should like to close with a number of questions which to me are vital and which I hope the minister will deem worthy of a reply. I hope the minister can inform this committee that the intentions of the government are as to when direct lending by C.M.H.C. is to be resumed. I know the minister is now making the beginning of the move asking for legislative authority. However, I also notice that in a bulletin entitled "National Home Builders Association Convention Report" dated January 12, 1960, on the last page it stated:
Don't expect direct government lending until later in year, probably in fall to boost winter building.
This was published only a month ago. The quotation continues:
The bill to increase direct lending has been drafted, but the exact amount has not yet been fixed.
We now have that amount in the resolution. The amount has been fixed. The quotation continues:
Best guess:	around $150 million. Walker
emphasizes that government will not go into direct lending until it sees what approved lenders do.
I hope the minister will reply to that because it is of considerable concern to those who are engaged in the construction industry. Is the report that the government is intending to do nothing with this money, even though it may be voted by this House of Commons, correct? Does it intend to sit back, see what private money lenders will do, and then maybe in the fall perhaps utilize the money that this house may be voting? There is concern in all parts of Canada as to how early this year the government is intending to make direct loans in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OP INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to thank the hon. member and say that he is under some misapprehension. The magazine he was reading

National Housing Act
from is the N.H.B.A. magazine and they are referring to builders loans. It has not been the policy of our government to make any builders loans except in the winter months of 1958 and 1959. There certainly have never been any builders loans at the beginning of the year and we have no knowledge or thought of making any at the present time.
The home owners loans-that is, the direct loan from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to the home owner who would like to build a house-will commence again when this legislation is through. That is one of the reasons why it is far up on our legislative program.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OP INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I thank the minister for his prompt reply, but I regret very much that it is not the intention of the government to make the builders loans available. Because I believe the minister must realize from the statistics which are available to him and from advice he is getting that we are running into a dead end and that action now is needed as it has never been needed before.
Here I come to another matter which I hope he will deal with in his reply, and it has to do with the insured loans referred to in the resolution. What reason has the government to expect that there will be any more private funds available as a result of either this forecasted legislation or the raise in interest rates? I have here a press clipping from one of the newspapers in my province which, upon the announcement of the minister of an increase in the interest rate, had this to say:
N.H.A. rate boost not likely to aid loans.
A boost in N.H.A. interest rates is unlikely to stimulate the new capital hoped for by the federal government, according to Vancouver lending institutions.
In the N.H.B.A. bulletin I referred to before there is a headline which says that this battle for money is to be fierce in 1960. Among other things it says that house build-ders this year face the toughest battle for mortgage money ever fought in Canada. It goes on:
Recent hike in the N.H.A. interest rate (now standing at six and three quarters per cent) won't help as much as the increase three years ago. There's just too much competition for money at more remunerative rates.
That brings to mind an advertisement I saw in the Ottawa Citizen of February 1, an offering by Wood, Gundy and Company Limited, and the headline is: "Over 6 per cent yield from Ontario hydro bonds". I think if the minister compares the value of Ontario hydro bonds with the value of housing paper even he would be unwilling to lend what money he has for purposes of

housing at 6f per cent if he could obtain in excess of a 6 per cent yield from Ontario hydro bonds, with even the possibility of a capital gain should the Minister of Finance continue in office much longer and the bond market continue to deteriorate.
I feel that 6f per cent is unrealistic if it is intended to lure more private money into the housing field. If that is its intention, in order for it to be a realistic rate it ought to be much nearer seven and a half per cent, if not 8 per cent, and heaven forbid that I would support such a move. However, I feel in this respect that the government has its head in the sand, because people can now buy top notch first class mortgages, in the lower mainland of British Columbia at least, and obtain a yield of 8 and 9 per cent.
I am on the board of directors of a cooperative housing association. We have millions of dollars on our books in first mortgages at 8 per cent, and the demand for money from our resources is endless. Six and three quarters per cent is a most unrealistic rate. It is merely an attempt to avoid admitting the inevitable, that lending institutions as presently constituted on the national economic scene cannot be induced to make the necessary funds available for housing at rates of interest that average wage earners are able to afford.
It is no use for the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance to be clubbing the management of the banks or Canadian investment companies. This situation exists and it has to be faced. In the field of housing I feel that with the unwillingness of the government to take other action the only thing I can recommend is that this Conservative government adopt the attitude that, for those of less than average income, housing has become a social responsibility, and with the Conservatives of today willing to adopt the concept of the welfare state, I do not think my plea should fall on completely deaf ears. I feel that the Conservatives may yet perform many a miracle in order to survive in office; and while the Prime Minister's government is now to the left of the former government, circumstances may make it move much further to the left yet before it ever sets the stage for the next election in Canada, despite the intentions of the hon. member for Essex East and the rest of the Liberal party in this respect. I wish to raise one other matter, and that is that I feel municipalities are most unfortunate in not being able to take the initiative in the matter of housing. Over the years I have heard hon. member after hon. member rise in his place and castigate municipal authorities for not taking advantage of

certain sections of the National Housing Act. In this regard I feel that the municipalities are blameless because I am sure they would love to take advantage of the many portions of the act which are designed for initiative to be taken on their part. However, municipalities, especially the growing ones, have tremendous responsibilities in regard to capital costs. They have to provide new sidewalks, sewers, water mains, schools and hospitals, and they feel that taking the initiative in the matter of low cost housing is beyond the realm of possibility.
This is why I believe that the matter which I raised on orders of the day is so vital. The government should take steps to reactivate, among other things, the Municipal Assistance Improvements Act so that municipalities would have low cost money available to them and be able to take an interest in the act and engage in such projects as land assembly, which would be to the benefit of all potential home owners in Canada and also those people who are interested in the orderly development of housing within the municipalities.

In commencing what I have to say on this subject, I certainly wish to congratulate the minister on his appointment. I have no doubt he will succeed in accomplishing the tremendous tasks he has before him and will follow the precedent established by his predecessor who was without doubt the greatest minister of public works this country has ever known. I speak not only of the benefits which have come to my own riding, although this government, through the Department of Public Works, has done more, spent more and accomplished more in my riding in two years than all the other governments since confederation.
How about unemployment?

I will come to unemployment but we are speaking on housing this afternoon and I should like to discuss one or two of the problems which have arisen in connection with housing as I have come to know them.
Last year I took the trouble to go to England to study the housing system there. I also took the trouble to study the plan which operates in the United States and in other countries. I may say that when you go to buy a house in the United States the first thing that strikes you on entering is that the house comes equipped with up to $2,000 worth of built-in kitchen equipment. This is most important to a family starting out in life. The house comes equipped with a built-in refrigerator, oven, stove, washer and dryer.
National Housing Act
In some cases there are built-in items which we would even regard as luxuries here but which, nevertheless, are included in the total price of the house. The house may cost $14,000, but a man can purchase it for something like $450 down. If he is a veteran, he pays nothing down. This enables a family starting out in life on a low income to acquire a home which is already almost fully equipped. The only further items needed are bedding, furniture and equipment for the dining room and living room. The house, as I say, comes sufficiently equipped to permit a family to start housekeeping for a minimum deposit of something like $400 and, in the case of a veteran, no deposit at all is needed.
I found out that the approach in England is along the same lines. Over there the government has seen to it that houses are financed almost 100 per cent. I was amazed at the complete effectiveness when I began to study the housing situation in England.
Here in Canada, this is what happens, and I know whereof I speak from personal experience, having been concerned with housing developments and in other phases of real estate. Not only does a couple need to make a down payment of $2,000, $3,000 or $4,000- and it usually works out that a family needing a house in Canada has to find something like $3,500-but the house, when purchased contains no built-in equipment to speak of.
I am telling you, Mr. Chairman, that as far as the great majority of our young families in this country are concerned they do not have that kind of money to put down. This is what happens: They get it from the finance companies, or from the oil companies who take a second mortgage on the house. I know that to be a fact. Many of the oil companies will go to a builder and say: let us handle your second mortgage in return for the business of supplying the oil furnace in the basement. The family might succeed in getting $1,000 to put down. The oil company takes a second mortgage, and after a lot of difficult manoeuvring the family succeeds, after obtaining a loan from the finance company, a note from the builder, and a mortgage from the oil company, and the initial loan from the C.M.H.C., in taking possession of a house. What is the result? That family is in hock for the first five years after moving into the house, and this applies to 67 per cent of the people in Canada who-buy houses under the present system.
I feel this is placing too great a burden upon our people. All I am asking is that this government should place as much confidence in the people of Canada as the United

National Housing Act
States government places in the American people. If the United States government can show such confidence, then, surely, we can do the same. Right off the bat, I mention this: I realize that this over-all plan of housing is the usual result of niggardly Liberal thinking which evolved our housing plan in the first place, and I have no doubt that every member of this government is more than sympathetic with regard to the plight of those who cannot purchase a house under the existing system in Canada. In the United States a value of up to 96 per cent is recognized on a house which has already been built, thus insuring that people who have houses not built under the housing plan are protected, and loans of up to 96 per cent of their value are available to them when they want to sell or buy these houses.
I had an experience with regard to one project where there were 104 applicants for 100 houses. This had nothing to do with any personal business of mine. Out of the 104 applicants, only one person was able to make the down payment. However, one oil company was prepared to put up a second mortgage on each of the houses for $1,500 on condition they got the oil business. I remember discussing this problem one day with a very good businessman in Canada, and I was telling him that if only our government could realize that they should have the same confidence in the Canadian people as the United States government has in the American people the situation would work out very well. He said: Mr. Van Horne, you can tell your government one thing more on that score. If the government of Canada had as much confidence in Canada as the United States has in Canada we would be much better off.
Who needs a house? I respectfully submit that it is the young married couple starting out in life who need to have a house built under our plan. Some people may say that it is wrong to buy a house by way of a second mortgage or to carry out secondary financing. But this is exactly what is being done in more than 67 per cent of the cases. The government, if it wishes, can ascertain whether that figure is correct. In a survey which my company carried out on five different projects scattered in five different localities the figure amounted to 67 per cent. What is so wrong with the United States plan of permitting people to enter a house on a minimum payment of $400 or $500, and

what is so wrong with permitting a veteran to purchase a house without a down payment?
If the United States government can do it, as it has done since 1944, do you mean to tell me that this government cannot do it? This problem is not insurmountable.
If it was something that was not of immediate importance not only to the people of my riding but to all people across Canada whose incomes are below $5,000 a year, I would not be pressing as I have been during the four years I have been a member of the house that the government adopt the same system that exists in the United States. It may be said that we are building quite a few houses in Canada. That may be true but let us not forget that under the United States system the people there have been able to acquire their homes years ago whereas under our system housing has not been available to our people because of the high down payments.
What is so wrong about acknowledging the lending value of a house that is already built even though the house was not built under the National Housing Act? If there were not an example right across the border I would not be pressing as I am and have been.
But here is what really discourages a member of parliament. I go down to Mada-waska county in my riding and meet some very fine citizen in the town of St. Leonard, let us say, who lives only 500 feet from the state of Maine. He says to me, "Mr. Van Horne, what is wrong with you people in Ottawa? Why is it that John Jones who lives 500 feet from me across the line can buy a beautiful house for nothing down because he is a veteran and I have to dig up $4,000 which I have not got and cannot get because I am not earning a salary that will ever permit me to save it"? He says, "Why is it that you want to penalize us"? I tell him, of course, that we are still suffering from the influence of the old Liberal regime.
You were only in office two years.

I certainly sympathize with these people. It is all very well for this little gentleman over there, this hon. member, to make these remarks, but let me assure him that if he were face to face with the people who need housing and cannot get it he would not interject as he does. I

am going to bring this up on another occasion but in my office I have a collection of probably a hundred pictures of slum dwellings that exist, home dwellings. I have gone to see these families. They could find $700 or $800 to put down on a house but they cannot find $3,500 or $4,000. They are people who work in the woods. They are smart people and all they ask is a chance.
There is no difference between these people who live in Madawaska county and the people who live in Maine. If the people of Maine who are only 350 feet away can have housing available to them for $300 or $400 down and in the case of veterans nothing down, I sincerely suggest and submit to the government for its consideration, and I trust it will consider these things now, that the solution of our housing problem in Canada is not as difficult as far too many of the people in the government wish to make it. We can solve the problem, by adopting lock, stock and barrel the U.S. system. All that is needed is more confidence on the part of this government in the Canadian people.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, before starting the few remarks I would like to make on this resolution, I want to take this opportunity of tendering my sincere congratulations to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), on the occasion of his appointment to one of the most important federal departments. I also wish him good luck and good health, because I know from experience the numerous and heavy responsibilities which are now resting upon his shoulders.
I also would like to congratulate his new parliamentary secretary (Mr. Tasse) who, like myself, is a former student of the "Ecole polytechnique" in Montreal. The minister will certainly be able to rely on him as a helper in his work. I am sure that, being an engineer, he will be very valuable to the minister, more particularly in a department where technical and engineering problems so frequently come up.
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of the resolution is to amend the National Housing Act of 1954, and as it says:
-to increase the aggregate amount of all loans in respect of which insurance policies may be issued under the act from four billion dollars to six billion dollars; and to increase from one billion dollars to one and a half billion dollars the aggregate amount that may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund for the purposes specified in subsection 1 of section 22 of the said act.
National Housing Act
Mr. Chairman, I am convinced, as is the minister, that all hon. members recognize the importance of the housing issue, from an economic as well as from a social point of view. As far as I can remember, since the National Housing Act was adopted, I have always been pleased to note that all hon. members, from all parties represented in the house, and, in spite of divergent views as to the methods of application, always favoured any legislation that would improve the housing position in this country.
During the discussions of this matter in the past, I always expressed the opinion that, in spite of an increase of available funds and some minor amendments, the National Housing Act failed of what was its main objective at the time it was introduced, that is, to provide a decent home for every Canadian.
If I was right on this point in the past,. I am doubly so today, if we consider that the rate of interest which, formerly, or rather before last October, was 6 per cent has now been established at 6| per cent for all insurable loans which, under this act may be granted by private lenders and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Moreover, we must remember that today limited dividend corporations, whose object it is to build low rental housing for our senior citizens and people of low income, will find their task more difficult and costly, because, since October 1, 1959, the interest rate on those loans has been increased from 5| per cent to 5| per cent.
May I say then that the optimism and enthusiasm about housing, which, according to the former minister of public works, now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green), was again noticeable throughout Canada, is more and more on the wane.
This is readily seen in the figures of table 20 in the report for the third quarter of 1959 entitled "Canadian Housing Statistics".
We find, for instance, that the number of mortgage loans authorized under the National Housing Act and made by lending institutions as of the second quarter of 1958, reached 18,901, while it stood at 13,850 only during the second quarter of 1959.
If we look at the figures for the third quarter, the difference is even greater: for the third quarter of 1958, there were 14,345 loans, while in the same quarter for 1959, there were only 5,781.

National Housing Act
And if we refer to table 21 in the same report, we see that for the first eleven months of 1958, there were 44,675 mortgage loans authorized under the National Housing Act by category of lenders, while the number was down to 26,504 for the eleven month period ending in November 1959. On the other hand, C.M.H.C. loans remained practically at the same level.
Table 24 of the same booklet also gives a fair idea of the decreasing amount of loans made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to limited dividends corporations, since, according to that table, in the third quarter of 1958, loans had been made for 2,927 units, while, in the course of the third quarter of 1959, 457 loans only were made.
Mr. Chairman, it will perhaps be asked what were the reasons for this decrease. Well, in my opinion, they are obvious. It appears that, early in 1959, there was a substantial decrease in the number of direct loans made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Furthermore, corporations or lending institutions shied away from housing loans, because of the high rates of interest on government bonds.
But in my view, the most important factor in the slowdown of housing was the tight money situation prevailing in 1959, a situation which still exists today. Tight money, of course, was caused by the many deficits of the government since its assumption of power, by the many government loans, and particularly by the famous loan floated in the fall of 1958.
I mentioned early in my remarks that the recent rise from 6 to 6J per cent in the interest rate will cause a reduction in housing. Mr. Chairman, I am not alone in this view. I do not know whether the minister has had an opportunity, since his appointment as Minister of Public Works, to go over the high-sounding speeches made by his friends when they sat on this side of the house; if he did, he would have seen, for instance, what the present Minister of Finance used to think about the increase in the interest rate. Here is something he said on April 23, 1956, as recorded on page 3171 of Hansard:
I am bound to point out that an increase in the interest rate normally has the effect and usually is intended to have the effect-
And this is important. I am not sure the minister will take up this point.

-of restraining house construction.
I wonder, therefore, whether the present government, in raising the interest rate, is striving to slow down construction.
On page 3307 of Hansard for the same year, the Minister of Finance made another statement, and you should have heard how forcefully he expressed himself. I quote:
The effect of an increase in interest rate necessarily is to make construction more expensive, to increase carrying charges, and to that extent to reduce the volume of home construction that would otherwise be attained ... The government cannot escape its responsibility in this respect.
I must point out to the minister that at the time, when the Minister of Finance talked about high interest rates, the rate was only 5J per cent, not 6j per cent as it is today.
Let us see now what the former minister of public works, the predecessor of my hon. friend, thought of the tight money situation and its effects on housing construction. Here is what he said on May 15, 1958, according to page 116 of Hansard:
We had not been in office very long before we found that there was a rapid falling off in housing construction across Canada. Lending institutions were advancing money reluctantly because of the tight money policy then in effect and this tight money policy was hitting the building industry harder than any other industry in the country. It was fairly easy to get a loan for an expensive home but it was very hard to get one for a small home.
It would be interesting also, Mr. Chairman, to recall what the Prime Minister thought of the tight money situation and its effect on housing construction. I have here a copy of an article published in the Toronto Telegram of October 30, 1957, entitled: "Credit where needed", and from which I quote:
(Text):
In the Prime Minister's opinion, the adverse effects of tight money have been most severe among persons interested in low and middle cost housing. In this area, he said, "credit restrictions had virtually nullified the rights of prospective home owners under the National Housing Act". Not only was tight money creating unemployment, it was impeding the normal development of our most precious asset-the average young Canadian family.
(Translation) :
Well, Mr. Chairman, if those people who now wield most influence in the cabinet and now have to find a solution to this problem, could then blame the government of that time, can we not tell them today that they are not logical, because of their past attitude and mainly because they forget the promises they made about this and many other matters.

That is why I repeat what the Minister of Finance said then:	The government cannot
shirk its responsibilities in this matter.

Questions
The following answers, deposited with the Clerk of the house, are printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT APPLICATION, OTTAWA RESIDENTS
speechtext:
1.	Did the civil service commission, within the last six months, solicit applications for employment in the Department of National Revenue from Ottawa residents?
2.	If so, how many letters or circulars were sent out, and what was the estimated cost of the preparation and printing of such material?
3.	Were newspaper advertisements used in an attempt to recruit personnel for these particular positions?
4.	If so. what was the cost of such newspaper advertisements?
Answer by: Hon. Leon Balcer (Acting Secretary of Stale):
1.	The civil service commission, in October 1959, distributed circulars through the Post Office Department to all house holders within a 35 mile radius of Ottawa, for part-time employment in the taxation division, Department of National Revenue.
2.	135,000 circulars were sent out at a cost of $990.42 for preparation and printing.
3.	To supplement the advertising by means of the special announcement circulars, an advertisement was inserted in the Ottawa newspapers on October 22, 1959.
4.	The cost of a 3" deep classified display advertisement in the Ottawa Citizen, The Journal, and Le Droit totalled $26.76 for one insertion.

1* Since the beginning of the current fiscal year, have phase tenders for any one project been asked by the Department of Public Works?
2. If so, what are the projects, and for what reasons have phase tenders been called?
Answer by: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of
Public Works):
1.	Yes.
2.	Jackson Building, Ottawa-Rehabilitation after explosion.
Due to the serious damages caused by an explosion during the fall of 1958, immediate action had to be taken to restore the building to its previous standard with the least possible delay to provide accommodation for the departments previously occupying this building.
The remedial work was divided into four phases to allow as many of the original
occupants to return while repairs were being effected. The four phases were:
1.	Restoration of the exterior walls, openings and elevator services.
2.	Repairs to the interior including partitions on the first three floors.
3.	Repairs to the interior including partitions and lighting on the six remaining floors (4 to 9 respectively).
4.	Repairs to the plumbing, fire protection system and the cafeteria.
A contract was issued for each phase after receipt of public tenders. The work on phases 1 and 2 is completed; the work on phase 3 is 98 per cent completed and work on phase 4 is in progress.
Preparation of plans and specifications for the whole remedial work with the intention of obtaining one tender call would have seriously delayed reoccupation of the building. The procedure taken permitted the planning of each phase while work was being proceeded with on the previous phase and resulted in the reoccupation of the whole building in less time than if the project had been awarded to one general contractor.
Examining warehouse, 326 Howe street, Vancouver, B.C.-Major repairs and renovations.
This building which was mostly occupied by the Post Office Department became vacant after the personnel of that department was transferred into the new post office building completed during 1958. Major repairs were required to provide better and proper accommodation for numerous government departments including transport, citizenship and immigration, public printing and stationery, finance, northern affairs and national resources, national health and welfare, agriculture and the unemployment insurance commission, most of which were occupying rented quarters at various locations in the city of Vancouver.
The phasing of this repair and improvement work was instituted in order to provide the urgently required accommodation as soon as possible, rather than have these offices ill-housed until the whole of the alterations were completed.
During May, 1959, after receipt of public tenders, a contract was awarded for major repairs on the first, second, third and fourth floors of this building including the installation of a new freight elevator and a fish testing laboratory. The work is nearly completed.
During December, 1959, after receipt of public tenders, a contract was awarded for additional repairs on the second and third floors. This work is in progress.

Hamilton, Ontario-Harbour improvements.
Hamilton harbour has a long history of continued growth in traffic. It has been necessary to expand facilities for the freight traffic at public wharves in both the bulk and general cargo quantities. An expansion program was started in 1955, in conjunction with the Hamilton harbour commissioners and, since that time, the major projects completed or presently under way include the Wellington street dock and transit terminal, the ship street terminal 3 development, Strathearne avenue development, and the Burlington beach wharf. These structures will all meet seaway requirements as to available depth and berth size.
During 1959-60, the following stages of work were under way: stage 1, Burlington beach wharf, berm construction; stage 2, Burlington beach, dredging; stage 3, Strathearne avenue, wharf face walls and dredging.
It is anticipated that the above works will all be completed during the coming fiscal year.
Lakehead (Port Arthur and Fort William, Ontario)-Harbour development.
In order to serve western Canada with a port on the great lakes system capable of handling the deep draft ocean freighters, a multistage development program was started at the lakehead. The project calls for the construction of a modern seaway terminal with rail and storage facilities and other ancillary services. When complete, this terminal should offer one of the most efficient general cargo handling depots in Canada. Near the boundary between Port Arthur and Fort William, a large area of land is being reclaimed as the construction site to be developed.
During 1959-60, the following stages were under way; stage 1, construction of bridges and access roads, completed; stage 2, dredging and reclamation, reclamation completed and dredging transferred to stage 3; stage 3, construction of wharf and substructure, contract documents being reviewed prior to tender call; stage 4, additional fill and stockpile, work under contract not yet commenced.
Further stages of the over-all project will be initiated as the planning is completed.
Toronto, Ontario-Harbour improvements.
During the last several years, improvements have been made to provide the channels of this harbour with seaway depths. The department has been concerned primarily with dredging in the approach and entrance channels, while the Toronto harbour commission has been responsible for most of the construction work on new terminals, etc.

Dredging, inner eastern harbour, not completed. 2. Dredging, eastern channel (clean up), completed.
In addition, dredging in the western entrance channel continued, with the spoil being used on the Toronto island airport extension work which this department has undertaken for the Department of Transport. On the airport extension project, we have been concerned mainly with the construction of retaining bulkheads.
St. John's, Newfoundland-Harbour reconstruction.
One of the largest harbours and rivers engineering projects ever undertaken by the department has been the improvement project at St. John's, Newfoundland, which includes the over-all renovation of a large section of the waterfront. The work includes the construction of a new general cargo handling terminal, additional deep-water and coastal shipping berths, new transit sheds, and the provision of both open and covered storage space. In addition, new service roads, sewer extensions, modern handling equipment, etc., are planned.
To date, five major parts of the project have been completed or are under way:
1.	Construction of Department of Transport marine agency wharf-completed.
2.	Small boat basin-completed.
3.	Dredging-completed, but a portion of the dredging was transferred to the main terminal contract.
4.	Removal of SS Desola-contract just awarded and work to start directly.
5.	Main terminal pier-contract awarded recently and work now under way.
In addition to the above projects, a number of smaller demolition contracts have been awarded, with some completed. These works include the demolishing of private dwellings, commercial buildings, sheds and wharves.
Other major portions of the project, which will be started as the planning permits, include:
1.	Transit shed, warehouse and administration building construction.
2.	Completion of the north shore embankment wall.
3.	South shore service road.
4.	Construction of the C.N.R. newsprint pier.
5.	Installation of rail and other services.

subsubtopic: PERSONNEL STATISTICS
speechtext:
How many salaried civil servants were in the employ of the federal government as at the end of December, 1959, and at the end of December, 1958?
Answer by: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister
of Trade and Commerce):
Statistics for December, 1959 are not yet available. The latest figures available are for September, 1959 and show:
Salaried civil servants* in the employ of the federal government: September, 1958, 153,859; December, 1958, 154,311; September, 1959, 155,950.
*"Salaried" employees include all persons paid on the basis of an annual salary rate and occupying salaried positions authorized by the treasury board or the privy council with the exception of government ships' officers.

maintopic: CANADIAN SUPPLY AND EQUIPMENT REQUIREMENTS, NATO
CANADIAN SUPPLY AND EQUIPMENT REQUIREMENTS, NATO
speechtext:
1.	Are all supply and equipment requirements of Canadian forces in NATO met by open contract within the NATO infrastructure?
2.	If so, what portion, in value, has been provided by Canadian suppliers for each year in the last five years?
3.	If not, what is the distinction or line between material supplied by Canada to its forces and that which comes from other sources?
Answer by: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister
of Nafional Defence):
1, 2 and 3. The NATO infrastructure program concerns the provision of fixed facilities and not supplies and equipment. The supplies and equipment for the Canadian forces in Europe are obtained mainly from Canadian sources, except for certain items which are obtained for reasons of economy and convenience from European sources (either through the procurement agencies of countries in which Canadian forces are stationed or through logistic support arrangements with the British army and the United States air force).
